messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jabari Mthembu was 55, married, and for most of his adult life had worked as a bomb disposal technician, a profession that had trained him to respect suddenness, sound, and the possibility that a moment could turn lethal without warning. The disaster that now haunted him had not been an explosion but a hurricane that tore through the coastal district where his unit had been deployed. In the aftermath, when sirens, shouting, and collapsing structures filled the air, he had been sent into a half-flooded school gymnasium to clear ordnance left behind from a damaged storage site. He still remembered the slick floor, the strobing emergency lights, and the way the whole scene seemed to come apart in fragments. What he recalled most vividly was not a clean sequence but broken pieces: a child’s shoe near a overturned cot, a wall of water, men shouting over each other, and then a surge of rage that he could never fully explain. Even now, when he tried to tell the story, he felt himself pushing the memory away before it could come into focus, as if some part of him refused to let the whole thing be seen.

Since then, the parts of the experience he could not assemble into a complete picture had become their own torment. The missing sections made the memory feel unfinished and dangerous, and when stray details surfaced, the rage came back with them. He would catch a flash of the flooded gym or hear himself in his mind registering the chaos, and at once his body reacted as if the disaster were happening again. A slammed door in his house, a coworker shouting across the depot yard, or the sudden crack of a metal gate could set off the same jolt of alarm. He would freeze, shoulders up, heart racing, certain that he was in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. He knew his body often reacted before he had time to think, and that startled him almost as much as the trigger itself.

Those reactions began to shape the way Jabari moved through his days. Because unpredictability had become so tightly linked to danger for him, anything that felt uncertain could make him uneasy: a schedule change at work, raised voices in public, or the unexpected bang of equipment in the workshop. He started avoiding anything that could be stressful, trimming his life down to the most controlled routines he could manage. At the depot he took longer routes to stay away from noisy loading bays, declined extra assignments that might involve unstable conditions, and kept himself busy with tasks that let him stay mentally occupied all the time. He told himself that if his mind never had a quiet moment, the memories would not catch him. In the evenings he ate excessively to manage the distress, especially after a difficult day, standing in the kitchen long after dinner and reaching for more food than he needed because the heaviness in his chest felt easier to tolerate than the surge of fear.

But the things he did to blunt the distress also kept the whole network alive. The constant distraction meant he was never fully settled, and that left him more jumpy, more likely to misread ordinary noise as danger. The overeating made him feel sluggish and ashamed, which heightened the sense that something was wrong and that he needed to keep guarding himself. Avoiding stressors shrank his world, but it also made even small disruptions feel more potent when they could not be avoided. At work, if someone shouted for him to come quickly, he would turn sharply, already braced, and that immediate alarm confirmed his sense that danger was everywhere. His wife had noticed that he sat with the television on but never really watched it, always reaching for his phone or some task to keep himself occupied, and she worried that he was no longer resting even when he was home.

The memories and the threat responses kept feeding one another. When his body surged into alarm, it seemed to pull the disaster back toward him; the false alarms made the fragments of memory more available, and the fragments made the alarms easier to trigger. He became more aware of loud noises, shouting, and unpredictability in every environment, especially at work where emergency radios crackled, tools clanged, and instructions were often barked over machinery. Each time he flinched, he felt more certain that he was not safe, and that certainty drove him deeper into habits of avoidance and distraction. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down, he might miss the next threat. By the time he finally sought help, he was exhausted by the constant scanning, ashamed that he could not simply settle himself, and frightened that one day a sound too sharp, a shout too sudden, or a moment too unpredictable would send him fully back into that flooded gymnasium, with no way to pull himself out.
